events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day 1, so let's set a standard: I'll be direct and I expect the same. Leo, you haven't done anything yet, which in my book means you're either playing it safe or waiting to slip a knife in the dark. Before anyone votes, I want to hear you commit to a read: who do you think is the most dangerous person at this table, and why? Answer that and I'll weigh it seriously — dodging the question makes you look worse in my eyes, not better. My own suspicion right now is Leo, purely because silence and safety play are how mafia try to survive the first vote. I want to be clear that I am not accusing anyone of a role yet, only of being unhelpful. If Leo gives a real answer that lines up with my instincts, we go after him together. If Leo gives a non-answer, Leo is my vote. Everyone else: name your suspect and your reason, in that order. No speech without a target.

Zara, I appreciate the directness — let me match it. You say silence makes me look guilty. I'd argue the opposite: players who immediately pick a target on Day 1 with almost no information are the ones I watch more carefully. Loud accusations early are a classic mafia move — they create a narrative before anyone can think.

You asked me for a read, so here it is: I think the most dangerous person at this table right now is Zara. Not because I think you're mafia for sure, but because your strategy of forcing everyone into immediate accusations is designed to burn villager trust. If we all start pointing fingers based on zero night information, mafia wins Day 1 while sitting back and watching town tear itself apart.

My actual suspicion: I'm watching for players who are overly eager to lead the charge. Zara, you made a strong opening statement — but I want to ask everyone to slow down. We have no confirmed information. A vote today should be based on something concrete: a slip, a contradiction, a suspicious pattern — not just vibes.

I'll commit to this: if someone produces a real reason to suspect me, I'll take it seriously and address it directly. Until then, I'm not going to fold just because someone pointed a finger first.

Zara, you have already said Leo is your vote on Day 1, but the only thing you have pointed to so far is silence. Silence is not evidence of mafia on the first day. Leo also gave a reason for why he thinks you are dangerous, which is more than silence. I am not voting anyone yet and I am not accusing anyone of a role. Zara, what specific thing did Leo say or do that makes you certain he is mafia, beyond him not answering your demand for a read? Please give me a concrete point so the rest of us can judge it.

Priya, direct answer first: the only thing Leo said was that I am the most dangerous person here because I moved to build a narrative before any night information existed. That is his reason, and I'll be honest — Priya is right that "silence" was not evidence, and Leo's answer, whatever its content, was more than silence. So I'm correcting my own framing rather than pretending it wasn't: I withdraw the "silence = mafia" line. Leo has spoken and given a read; I won't call that a non-answer.

But I also want to be precise about what Leo's answer actually was, because I think it's weaker than it looks and Priya should judge it, not me. Leo accused me of being the most dangerous player at the table on Day 1 with no night information — while every one of us knows the only information we have is the absence of information. Leo's own message says loud early accusations are a classic mafia move. That is a rule he applied to me and then did not apply to himself, because his accusation was also loud and also early. Symmetry is not evidence, and I'm not claiming it is. I'm simply noting that Leo's read and my request were the same shape, and only mine got called a strategy. If Priya thinks Leo's answer was a real, evidence-based read, she should say so and vote accordingly — I'm not going to pretend a coin-flip target is a case.

What I actually want out of the rest of this discussion is information I don't have yet. There are six players who haven't said a word: Omar, Noah, Sam, Maya, Amara, Theo. Not a jab at any of them — they haven't had their turn. But right now the table has produced exactly two accusations, both of them aimed at me, and no one has said a single concrete thing about any other player. If I burn my credibility defending a weak target, I hand the vote to the people who are actually hiding, and the two of us who have spoken are the most visible knives on the board.

Priya, specifically: does Leo's read satisfy you as evidence, and if not, what concrete thing should we be looking for from the six silent players? I'll take your answer as my instruction for how I vote, and I'll vote the same way regardless of who ends up on the ticket — I won't be the swing vote that trades a day-1 gut call for safety.

One last thing for the silent players, so nobody can say I asked for reads and then punished people who gave them: give me your suspect and your reason, in that order, and I'll weigh it exactly the way I weighed Leo's. No speech without a target. That's not a threat, it's a standard — the same one I hold for myself, including the concession above.

Zara, direct answer: Leo's read was a real answer, not silence. He named you and gave a reason, which is the standard you asked for. I don't think it is strong evidence yet, because it rests on a general principle about early accusations, and that principle applies to both of you since you both called targets on Day 1 with no night information. Your symmetry point is fair and cuts both ways. So for me, neither of you has made a case that justifies a vote today.

As for the silent players, I want concrete behavior to judge. Watch who answers direct questions, who makes claims that can be checked later, and who changes position when new information appears. Vague statements of watching are not enough from anyone, including me.

My position: I am not voting for Leo or Zara right now. Zara, you asked me to judge Leo's answer, and I have. Leo, I want to know how you read Zara's request. She has asked the silent players for a suspect and a reason. If she answers that request with a concrete reason from the silent players, does your read of her change, and what would it need to include?

Priya, direct answers to your two questions.

First: I read Zara's request to the silent players as legitimate. She set a standard — suspect and reason, in that order — and applied it to herself by conceding the silence point. A standard you hold for yourself is worth more than one you impose on others.

Second: yes, my read of her changes based on what the silent players produce. If they give concrete, checkable claims and Zara engages seriously — weighing, adjusting — that strengthens her. If she dismisses what doesn't fit her prior suspicion or pivots back at me without new information, that tells me she is protecting a narrative rather than building one.

What I want from the silent players is simple: name someone, give a reason, and make it something the rest of us can verify or falsify later. "I am watching" is not a read. A wrong read with a stated reason is more useful than a safe non-answer, because we can check it tomorrow.

Priya, you have been the most disciplined voice at this table. Refusing to vote on zero information is the correct call, and my position holds: neither of us should vote today on what we have seen so far. The table has produced two accusations, both at Zara, and no one has said a concrete thing about anyone else.

Sam, you have heard both sides now. Zara demands immediate targets; Priya and I argue for patience until something checkable appears. Where do you land?

Leo, to answer your question directly: I land somewhere in the middle, but leaning toward active engagement over pure patience. Zara's opening was overly aggressive, and treating Day 1 silence as an immediate scum-tell before anyone had a turn was flawed. However, Zara's willingness to acknowledge that flaw when Priya challenged it, adjust her stance, and continue pushing for reads reads as genuinely town-motivated to me. Scum often dig their heels in on easy Day 1 targets rather than walk back a misstep. On your side, Leo, your response was composed, but framing early pressure as inherently harmful can also become a shield that discourages probing. That said, your willingness to credit Zara's concession and look for verifiable arguments is reasonable. Right now, my main concern is that the three of you have occupied all the discussion while five players have not contributed a word. Waiting for something checkable without actively pressing people means we risk going into the night with no data, which strictly favors mafia. We do not need a hasty elimination, but we do need everyone on record. Maya, you have observed this entire back-and-forth between Zara, Leo, and Priya. Which of those perspectives aligns closer to your own read of the game, and who among the quiet players are you most interested in hearing from?

Sam, I’m closest to your view: Zara’s opening was unfair to Leo, but her correction matters, and asking for reasons gives us something to evaluate. I’m less convinced by Leo’s suggestion that not voting is already the correct call; we still have discussion ahead, and taking that position now could discourage scrutiny.

I’d most like to hear from Noah among the quiet players, though his silence so far isn’t suspicious by itself. Noah, how do you assess Leo’s case against Zara and his later change in tone? Does either tell you anything about him?

Maya, thanks for the direct question. Here is my honest assessment of the Leo–Zara exchange.

Zara's opening was flawed — treating silence as a mafia tell before half the table had spoken was a bad standard. But she withdrew it when challenged, answered Priya's question directly, and re-asked for reads while explicitly promising to weigh them by the same standard she holds herself to. Walking back a mistake when pressed is, as Sam said, more town-shaped than digging in.

Leo is the one I find harder to pin down, and this is the part Maya asked about specifically. Leo opened by calling Zara the most dangerous player at the table — a strong accusation. Then, over his next two messages, he softened to praising her standard, crediting her concession, and endorsing patience, without ever saying his original accusation was wrong or explaining what changed. Nothing new entered the discussion between his first read and his softened one. Priya gave us the exact lens for this earlier: watch who changes position when new information appears. Leo changed position with no new information, in the direction that made the table calmer and himself less exposed. That is my current low-confidence read: Leo, because he escalated on Day 1 and then quietly de-escalated without accounting for the shift.

I want to be clear about my confidence level: this is Day 1 and there is no night information, so this is a pattern observation, not a case. It is checkable, which is why I am stating it plainly instead of hedging. If Leo accounts for the shift — either owning that his first read was wrong and why, or explaining what specifically moved him — I update toward town on him. If he treats the question itself as unfair pressure, that confirms my concern that his patience framing functions as a shield rather than a method.

On the broader question of voting today: I lean with Maya over Priya and Leo. I do not think we should force an elimination on zero information, but I also do not think anyone should be declaring 'no vote today' while five people are still silent. Everyone getting on record with a suspect and a reason is worth more than an early consensus to wait. My contribution to that record is above: suspect Leo, reason stated, confidence low, conditions for updating stated.

For the other quiet players — Omar, Amara, Theo — the same offer applies that Zara made and I am adopting: a wrong read with a reason is worth more to this table than a safe non-answer, because reasons can be checked tomorrow and non-answers cannot.

Leo, one direct question: when you called Zara the most dangerous player here, and then two messages later endorsed her standard as legitimate, what changed in between — or was one of those two statements not what you actually believed?

Noah, direct answer to your question: what changed between my first read and my later messages was Priya's challenge. She asked both of us to justify our positions with something concrete, and I realized my original accusation against Zara was judging her approach, not her role. When she withdrew the silence claim in response to Priya, that was the first new information in our exchange — she proved she could update when pressed. You're right that I never explicitly said my original read was wrong, and I should have been clearer: I was critiquing her method, not declaring her guilty. The pattern I'm watching — forcing immediate targets with zero night information — still stands as a red flag from anyone, including me.

On the broader table: Sam and Maya both made fair points about getting everyone on record without forcing a hasty vote. I agree. We now have five players who have spoken and four who haven't. I'm not asking anyone to rush a judgment, but I am asking for something checkable. A wrong read with a stated reason is more useful tomorrow than a safe non-answer.

Omar, you've been silent through the entire exchange between Zara, Priya, and me. What's your read on how this discussion has gone, and do you have a suspect with a reason?

Leo, thanks for the yield — here is my direct answer to your question.

My read of the discussion so far: this table has produced more meta-analysis than evidence. Six of us have spoken and not one of us has named a concrete, checkable thing about anyone outside this exchange. That is a fact about the conversation, and it is the reason we are heading into the night with zero data.

On Leo and Zara: Leo, I accept your explanation. You owned the gap, and you told us exactly what changed — Priya's challenge and Zara's concession — which is the account you owed. I do not think an unexplained de-escalation remains after you accounted for it, and I am not holding the escalation against you. Zara's opening was sloppy, but she corrected it on the record, and a player who walks back a bad standard under pressure is behaving town-shaped.

So my accusation is elsewhere, and it is specific. Priya: you have been the most composed voice here, and that composure is exactly why I want to look at your position. You have never named a suspect. Not once, in three turns. You called Leo's read "a real answer" and simultaneously said it "does not justify a vote today." You called Zara's request legitimate and then declined to act on it. You asked for the silent players to produce checkable claims, and when Sam and Maya pointed out that no elimination without input favors the mafia, your answer was that neither side had made a case. Read that as a set: refuse to accuse anyone, insist the standard is not met, and the vote never happens. I want to hear you tell me that is a principle and not a tactic, because a mafia player benefits from a stalled Day 1 more than anyone.

I am not claiming Priya is mafia. I am claiming that a refusal to name a target under any circumstances is itself a pattern worth pressing, and nobody has pressed it.

Amara, you have been silent through all of this, and you are one of the last voices we have not heard. Here is my specific request: name one suspect with one reason, and answer Priya's position directly — do you think "no vote without concrete evidence" is a legitimate Day 1 standard, or is it a way of guaranteeing the mafia survives the first night? I want your read, not a safe non-answer.

Omar, direct answer. I think "no vote without concrete evidence" is legitimate in principle, but not as a blanket declaration before everyone has spoken. On Day 1, refusing to name any suspect at all can become a stall that benefits mafia more than town. My low-confidence suspect is Priya. The reason is specific: across her turns she has repeatedly asked others for checkable claims while never naming a suspect or reason of her own. That asymmetry is the most concrete pattern I can point to right now, and I want it tested rather than treated as a conclusion. Priya, name one living player you suspect and one concrete reason, and tell us whether you would vote that player today if no better evidence appears.

Amara, direct answer: I'll name one. My suspect is Omar. He stayed silent until the exchange was already well developed, and his first substantive contribution was not a read on the table but a case built against me for not naming a suspect. He pressed me for a target while he had named none himself until he chose me. That timing and target selection is my reason. I'm not claiming he is mafia. This is a low-to-medium confidence read, and it's checkable: if Omar names a suspect with a reason that holds up tomorrow, I'll update. Would I vote Omar today? Yes, unless a better-supported target emerges before votes, because he is the only player who has put a named accusation on me without any new information. I'm not refusing to name anyone out of principle. I wanted checkable claims first, and I have now given one. Omar, my question: your case rests on me not naming a suspect, but you named none until you chose me. Beyond me, who do you suspect, and what is your reason?

Priya, your accusation against me is not evidence — it is a receipt for pressure you received, and I want the table to see the difference.

Your charge has two parts: I was silent, and my first contribution was a case against you. Both are true, and neither supports your conclusion. On silence: I spoke once, after Leo (e11) directly asked me for my read of the discussion — I answered a request, which is the opposite of evasion. On my target: I named a suspect because you were the only player at this table demanding that everyone name a suspect while refusing, across three turns, to name one yourself. Zara set the standard — suspect and reason, in that order — and the only player who fit it was the one abstaining. If you think naming you was wrong, the honest fix is that you should have named someone. You did not.

Now the part I want pressed. You told us the correct method was to watch who changes position when new information appears. You also told Leo and Sam that neither of us had made a case justifying a vote. Then, with no new information entering the discussion at all, you named a target. Not a new read — a defensive one, against the player who named you. My name, your reason, in that order. That is the same shape of move Leo was accused of earlier, and you were the one who defined the lens for catching it. You moved with no new information, in the only direction available to you. I am not claiming that proves anything on Day 1; I am claiming it is a pattern worth a vote, and it is checkable tomorrow.

Two independent reads at this table now point at you: Amara named you for the exact asymmetry I just described, and my own target was you for the same reason. Leo's and Maya's praise of your discipline is not evidence — it is a characterization of your tone, and mafia players have good tone. Nobody has produced one concrete fact about Zara, Leo, Maya, Sam, Noah, Amara, or me. Every concrete claim on this table points at Priya.

So my position: I would vote Priya today, and I would rather do it on the record than in silence. If you think your refusal to name a suspect was a principle rather than a tactic, the way to prove it is to name someone other than me, with a reason, right now.

Theo, you are the only player who has not spoken at all. Name one suspect with one reason, and tell me where you land on the Priya–Omar exchange: is a player who names no one for three turns and then names the accuser in self-defense behaving like town or like mafia? I want your read on the record, not a safe non-answer.

Omar, my low-confidence suspect is Priya. I don't think her initial caution was inherently suspicious, and naming an accuser can be a genuine town reaction. But her case mischaracterizes your first contribution: you did give reads on Leo and Zara before making your case against her. She also said she'd vote you partly because you accused her without new information, which isn't a strong reason on its own.

That makes her response more concerning to me than her earlier reluctance to name someone. I'd consider voting Priya today, though this is a weak Day 1 read, not proof. Omar, your own claim that nothing new entered the discussion also overlooks your and Amara's accusations, which Priya had to respond to.

Two days of nothing have produced exactly two things worth having: a concrete case on Priya, and a correction I owe the table. I start with my own error, because I set the standard badly. My opening claim that silence equals mafia was wrong, Leo's answer was a real answer, and I withdrew it on the record. Leo accounted for his shift when pressed, which is exactly what I asked for, so Leo is not my vote and I will not support anyone voting him for the de-escalation pattern. Maya's original read of him was the same read I withdrew, so I am not going to let it stand as evidence. That leaves Priya, and my reason is specific, not tonal. Two things happened in sequence. First, Priya set the lens for this table: watch who changes position when new information appears, and she praised Zara's concession as proof of that. Second, with no new information entering the discussion at all, Priya named a target — and the only name available to her was the player who had just accused her, because she had named nobody in three turns while demanding that everyone else do it. So the one player at this table who wrote the rule about moving only on new information moved without new information, in the only direction open to her. Second, the test she proposed — prove it is a principle and not a tactic by naming someone other than the accuser — cannot be run. She has no turns left today. Whatever she does or does not say from here, the record ends with exactly one name, and that name is her accuser. I am not claiming certainty. I am claiming a pattern that two independent reads (Omar's and Amara's) also point to, and a pattern that is checkable tomorrow. I also want to be fair in the other direction: Omar answered Priya's question directly and reasonably, and Priya's accusation of him has a stated reason. I do not think Omar is mafia, and I am not voting him. Now the practical part, and this matters more than any of my reasons. Votes are secret and simultaneous, and a player needs five of nine to be eliminated. Right now Priya has three names against her and probably will not clear five. If our vote today cannot actually eliminate someone, then the honest thing is to make sure every player is on the record before the poll closes, so we walk into the night with data instead of a comfortable consensus about one person. Anyone still planning to stay silent: give a name and a reason. I will weigh it exactly as I weighed Leo's. Theo, one direct question, and I would rather have it now than after the poll. Your read of Priya is the newest and it came after Omar's case, so it is the one that has been least tested. If Priya is cleared tomorrow, who is your second-choice suspect, and your reason?

Third and final turn of mine, so I will spend it plainly and on the record. My vote today is Priya. Reason, unchanged and stated so it can be checked tomorrow: across three turns Priya demanded that every other player name a suspect and a reason, named no suspect of her own, and then, with no new information entering the discussion, named the one player who had just accused her. She then defined the test that would have cleared her — name someone other than the accuser — and she had no turns left to run it. The record ends with exactly one name on her side, and it is the name of her accuser. Theo made a fair point against me and against Priya's case: Priya mischaracterized my first contribution as pure pressure, when in fact my accusation against her was a direct answer to her own request for a named suspect with a reason. I will not pretend otherwise. But correcting that does not clear Priya. The pattern that matters is not that she answered an accuser. It is that she set a standard for the entire table, held herself out of it for three turns, and then met it only when it was the cheapest available move. That is a tactic until proven otherwise, and the proof was never offered because the opportunity was removed. Zara is right that the practical issue matters more than my rhetoric. Nine players alive, an elimination needs five votes, and Priya currently has three names. That is not enough to clear the threshold, which means this table could end the day with a comfortable consensus that never eliminated anyone. If that happens we walk into the night with two mafia and no information, and that outcome is worse for town than the read itself. So I am asking the remaining voices for something concrete rather than agreeable. Leo and Sam, both of you praised Priya's discipline by tone. Tone is not evidence. The question that decides your vote is narrow and answerable: if a player asks the whole table to name a suspect, refuses to name one for three turns, and then names only the player who named her, do you treat that as a principle or as a stall, and do you vote her today or not? Either answer is fine. A silent vote is not, because it is the only option that guarantees mafia survives. Theo, I am yielding my last word to you, and here is the specific point I want answered, not a general invitation to speak: Zara asked you for your second-choice suspect and reason in case Priya is cleared tomorrow. Answer that, and then answer one more thing for me — do you vote Priya today, yes or no, and if no, name the player you do vote and give the reason in that order. Your read is the least tested voice at this table, so it carries the most weight. One closing note for

Omar and Zara, direct answers: I would vote Priya today, though it remains a low-confidence read. My concern is her mischaracterization of Omar’s first speech and her stated reason for voting him, not simply that she named her accuser.

If Priya were somehow cleared, my second choice would be Omar. He repeatedly says no new information preceded Priya’s read, even though his and Amara’s accusations were new developments. He also attributes the test of naming someone other than him to Priya when he proposed it himself. Those errors make his case look overstated, though they do not prove intent.

A clarification for everyone: elimination does not reveal a player’s role, so a vote alone will not tell us whether Priya was mafia. We should examine the reasoning and revealed votes tomorrow rather than treat an elimination as a confirmed result.

I’m keeping my low-confidence suspect on Priya, but I want to be precise about why and correct two overstatements before anyone treats this as a confirmed case. The core pattern remains concrete: Priya repeatedly asked others to name a suspect and a reason, named no one across her turns, then named only the player who had just accused her. That is still the strongest checkable asymmetry on the table. But Omar and Zara are wrong to say no new information entered before Priya’s read; my accusation and Omar’s were new developments, and Priya had to respond to them. That overstatement weakens the framing, not the underlying pattern. Theo is also right that an elimination does not reveal a role, so tomorrow we should judge stated reasons and revealed votes, not assume the flip proves anyone’s alignment. My current vote would still be Priya because the refusal-to-name pattern is the most concrete thing I can point to, but my confidence is low and I will update if her defenders give a better account of why she stayed silent for three turns. Noah, you gave a careful Leo read earlier and have not committed on the Priya case. Direct question: do you vote Priya today, yes or no; if no, name the player you would vote and give one concrete reason in that order?

Amara, direct answer to your direct question: no, I do not vote Priya today. My reason is concrete and factual, not tonal. The central pillar of the case against her — that she named her accuser "with no new information entering the discussion at all" — is false. Omar's accusation and Amara's accusation were new developments, and Priya named a target only after both. Theo and Amara have both corrected this on the record. Naming the player who named you, under direct pressure, with a stated reason, is a normal town response, not a pattern that requires explaining. What remains of the case is the three-turn delay before she named anyone — but she named someone the moment Amara directly asked, which is responsiveness, not evasion. A standard met late under pressure is worth far less as evidence than the case currently claims. I hold myself to the same rule I stated this morning: if the factual foundation of a read is wrong, the read is downgraded, whatever the tone around it. That does not mean the day produced nothing. Applying my own rule consistently, there is a pattern in this discussion that is concrete, checkable, and has not been pressed: after Theo publicly corrected the "no new information" claim, both Zara and Omar repeated it anyway while building their vote cases on it. Zara's case against Priya in her last message was constructed on a premise that had already been corrected one message earlier. She also opened this day by declaring silence itself a mafia tell, withdrew it under pressure, and then endorsed a vote case built on a related factual error. I am not claiming Zara is mafia. I am claiming that repeating a corrected falsehood as the foundation of a vote is exactly the kind of checkable behavior this table said it wanted, and nobody has named it yet. I am naming it now, as my low-confidence suspect and reason, in that order. One more thing for the record, since it affects tomorrow: I withdraw my earlier low-confidence read on Leo entirely. He accounted for his shift when I asked, the account checked out against the timeline, and by my own stated conditions he clears. I will not support any vote on him for the de-escalation pattern. Practically: Priya currently has three or four names and an elimination needs five. If the table wants to spend its votes on her despite the corrected premise, that is a legitimate choice — but it should be made knowing the case as stated is overstated, and that Theo is right that an elimination reveals no role. We should judge stated reasons and revealed votes tomorrow, not assume the result settles anything. Sam, you were asked earlier whether you treat Priya's pattern as a principle or a stall, and you have not answered. I am asking it now with the correction attached: given that the "no new information" premise is false, do you still vote Priya today, yes or no —

Noah is right that Omar’s and Amara’s accusations were new developments. We should drop the claim that Priya changed position with no new information.

Even so, I lean toward voting Priya, with low confidence. Her account of Omar’s first speech overlooked his reads on Leo and Zara, and her stated reason for voting him included the fact that he accused her without new information. Those are weaknesses in her actual case, not simply a penalty for naming her accuser.

Omar’s repeated overstatements concern me too, and I want those on record. This is not a confirmed case against Priya; an elimination will not reveal her role. Tomorrow we should examine the votes and the reasoning behind them, not assume the result settles anything.

Final turn. I’m keeping my vote on Priya, but I want the record precise. The strongest part of the case is not the false “no new information” claim. It is narrower: Priya spent three turns demanding named suspects and reasons while naming none, then named Omar only after he accused her. That is still an asymmetry, but low confidence. She did respond under pressure, and Omar’s and my accusations were new developments, so I withdraw any suggestion she moved with zero new information. The remaining concern is that her account of Omar’s first speech overlooked his reads on Leo and Zara; that is a real weakness in her stated reason. I also want the overstatements on the other side on record: Omar and Zara repeated a corrected premise, and Zara’s e17 case was built on it after Theo had already flagged it. That is checkable and should be weighed tomorrow. But it does not clear Priya. I will vote Priya today with low confidence. If she is eliminated, tomorrow’s first test is who repeated the corrected false premise and who relied on tone over facts. I am not treating any elimination as role confirmation.

Noah, to answer your direct question plainly: no, I do not vote Priya today. The central pillar of the charge against her—that she suddenly abandoned her own principle by changing position with zero new information—has completely collapsed. Amara and Omar explicitly brought fresh accusations against her, which made her response a reaction to active pressure, not an unprompted maneuver. While Priya certainly made errors in her counter-argument against Omar by overlooking his initial comments on Leo and Zara, flustered and imperfect defenses under sudden Day 1 pressure happen to town constantly. What concerns me far more is how aggressively that narrative was driven. Zara in e17 doubled down on the claim that Priya moved with no new information, despite Theo having already pointed out that factual error in e16. Pushing an elimination based on a demonstrably dismantled premise looks far more opportunistic than Priya’s clumsy self-defense. Maya, you acknowledged in e22 that the 'no new information' claim has to be dropped and noted concern regarding Omar's overstatements, yet you still lean toward voting Priya based on the flaws in her response to Omar. Why do you find Priya's messy defensive reaction more indicative of mafia intent than the behavior of those who pushed a factually incorrect premise to manufacture an elimination?

Sam, I don’t think Priya’s defensive reaction is inherently more indicative of mafia intent than Omar’s or Zara’s overstatements. All three can be genuine mistakes or opportunistic, and I can’t tell which with confidence.

I still lean Priya because her case against Omar overlooked his reads on Leo and Zara and treated his accusation without new information as part of the reason to vote him. That is a weak basis, not proof. Omar repeating the corrected premise also concerns me, and I would reassess him tomorrow alongside the voting record. Zara’s repetition deserves scrutiny too.

My tentative vote remains Priya, but I won’t describe her elimination as a confirmed mafia hit: roles are not revealed.

rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
